findings.reason: The protected SQL solution filters orders with invoice > 20, formats order_date to YYYY-MM month strings, and computes COUNT(order_id) as order_count and COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) as customer_count per month. The query runs in O(r log r) time and O(r) space; no candidate is required.

WHERE invoice > 20 strictly excludes orders with invoice <= 20 before grouping, ensuring months with no qualifying orders are omitted. COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) accurately counts unique customers per monthly group.

Filtering takes O(r) time. Grouping and computing distinct aggregates over r rows has a portable upper bound of O(r log r) time and O(r) auxiliary space. Complexity evidence is inherited and hash-bound.
Accepts Orders table and returns columns month (YYYY-MM format), order_count, and customer_count.

The approach accurately details WHERE clause pre-filtering, YYYY-MM month formatting, COUNT vs COUNT(DISTINCT) aggregate separation, and O(r log r) time / O(r) space bounds. Alternatives and edge cases cover separate year/month extraction, correlated monthly subqueries, conditional aggregation without filtering, strict invoice threshold enforcement, multi-order per customer counting, cross-month customer tracking, year-month distinction, empty qualifying months, and result ordering independence.

App SQL (SQLite strftime) and native SQL (MySQL DATE_FORMAT) solutions both execute the identical WHERE invoice > 20 GROUP BY month aggregation query with SHA-256 digests be8abd4d5d344c1f189580dd5c65eec718745cfe1d1877e427c085c2022eb476 and 809ee0ff0c0a63ca01588f4ba67f9c53be49cbd53f4657ef8031948b045f8322.
